one_liner: Rust stackful-coroutine runtime with Go-style go! and blocking-style I/O; its may_minihttp demo beat pre-1.0 tokio_minihttp by ~15% req/s.
what_it_does: May gives Rust goroutine-style concurrency: go! spawns a stackful coroutine, and may::net, may::sync and may::io offer blocking-style APIs (TcpListener/TcpStream, Mutex, MPMC channel, semaphore, timers, select, cancellation, coroutine-local storage) that park the coroutine instead of the OS thread. You write plain std-style code with no async/await, futures or Pin. It is not a Tokio replacement at the API level: Tokio-based crates (hyper, axum, tonic) need a Tokio runtime, and the caveat doc tells you to port dependencies to may-compatible versions, such as may_minihttp or may_postgres. may_minihttp, the benchmarked piece, is a small HTTP/1.1 server where you implement HttpService::call(&mut self, Request, &mut Response).
how_it_is_fast: Each coroutine runs on its own mmap'd stack (default 4K words = 32 KiB on 64-bit, with a PROT_NONE guard page) and switches through a hand-written assembly register swap from the generator crate, so a read that would block parks only the coroutine until epoll (Linux), kqueue (macOS/BSD) or IOCP (Windows) reports the socket ready, and the worker switches to the next ready coroutine. N worker threads (default num_cpus, pinned to cores by default) each run their own event loop with a local work-stealing queue, and finished coroutines are recycled through a pool (default capacity 1000). may_minihttp adds request batching: it reads all available bytes into a 32 KiB buffer, decodes every pipelined request with httparse, encodes all responses into one buffer and, on Unix, issues a single non-blocking write before waiting on the socket again.
when_to_use: You want Go-style thread-per-connection code in Rust (blocking reads/writes, mutexes, channels) at event-loop cost, without async/await function colouring.

HTTP/1.1 plaintext, JSON or Postgres-backed microservices where you control the whole stack: in TechEmpower Round 23 (Citrine, derived from raw data) may-minihttp ranked 1st of 518 on fortunes (1.33M rps), 2nd of 540 on JSON (3.10M vs hyper 2.89M, axum 2.71M) and 10th of 533 on network-bound plaintext (27.9M vs hyper 17.5M, axum 12.4M).
Porting an existing threaded, blocking Rust server where an async rewrite is too costly: swap std::net/std::sync for may::net/may::sync and wrap per-connection work in go!.
Many I/O-bound connections whose handlers need well under the 32 KiB default stack, on x86-64 or AArch64 Linux, macOS or Windows.
when_not_to_use: You depend on the Tokio ecosystem (hyper, axum, tonic, reqwest, sqlx): none of it runs on may's scheduler, and calling any thread-blocking API (std Mutex/Condvar, std::thread::sleep, blocking socket libraries) from a coroutine stalls the whole worker thread.
Millions of mostly idle tasks: every coroutine reserves a fixed stack that never grows (the author says 1M coroutines need at least 4 GB), while Tokio futures are stackless.

You need safe Rust to stay sound: touching thread-local storage across a yield is undefined behavior (libstd and C/C++ libraries use TLS), and open issue #109 argues go! hides the unsafe that spawn requires; the maintainer calls this intentional.

Deep recursion, large stack frames or heavy FFI engines: stack overflow hits the guard page and kills the process, and a user in #109 reports V8 and JavaScriptCore code silently not running or segfaulting inside coroutines.

Tail-latency-critical or thread-per-core designs: scheduling is cooperative (long CPU loops must call coroutine::yield_now()), there is no non-work-stealing mode and the author has no plan to add one (#90), and open issue #27 records much higher latency than Tokio in an early hyper port.

integration.dependencies: generator (stackful context switch), may_queue, crossbeam, parking_lot, socket2, core_affinity, smallvec, num_cpus, log, cfg-if; nix + libc on Unix; windows-sys on Windows. may_minihttp adds bytes, httparse, httpdate, itoa, once_cell.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition; may declares no rust-version, but its generator 0.8 dependency declares rust-version 1.73. README says stable, beta and nightly all work.
integration.platforms: x86_64 Linux/Windows/macOS and AArch64 Linux/macOS per the README (the generator crate also covers armv7, riscv64, loongarch64, ppc64le, s390x Linux, but may does not list them). I/O backends: epoll (Linux/Android), kqueue (macOS/BSD), IOCP (Windows).
integration.thread_safety: README: all coroutine APIs are safe to call from multiple threads. Coroutines migrate between worker threads via work stealing, so thread-local storage is not stable across yields; use coroutine_local! instead. Use may::sync primitives, not std::sync blocking ones, inside coroutines.

gotchas: go! wraps the unsafe coroutine::spawn in a hidden unsafe block, so safe-looking code can reach UB through TLS or FFI; call the unsafe spawn/Builder API directly if you want the unsafety visible.

Stack size is set in words, not bytes (set_stack_size(0x400) = 8 KiB on 64-bit). An odd stack size makes may pre-fill the stack and print the real usage when the coroutine exits; use it to tune. Functions with big stack frames such as std::io::copy are called out as risks.

may::config() (workers, stack size, pool capacity, worker pinning, poll timeout) takes effect only before the scheduler starts; workers are pinned to CPU cores by default (set_worker_pin(false) to turn it off).
An I/O-ready coroutine keeps reading until the socket returns WouldBlock before it yields, which the author links to latency jitter under load (#27).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick may over monoio when you want multi-threaded work stealing and blocking-style std-like code on Linux, macOS and Windows rather than thread-per-core io_uring with async/await (monoio's own echo benchmark shows a larger 1.86x edge over Tokio, but may_minihttp has the stronger independent TechEmpower record). Pick it over futures-based Tokio challengers such as exec-rs or Rain when you would rather avoid async entirely; for C++, PhotonLibOS is the closest stackful-coroutine analogue.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran wrk (1 client thread, 200 connections, 10 s) against the hello-world servers of may_minihttp and tokio_minihttp with one server worker thread on an unspecified laptop: 116,182 vs 100,651 req/s (~1.15x), with lower average latency (1.70 ms vs 1.98 ms) but higher max latency (20.17 ms vs 12.53 ms); the Tokio side is tokio-core/tokio-proto 0.1 on futures 0.1, and neither rustc version nor CPU is stated. Independent TechEmpower data is framework-vs-framework, not a clean Tokio comparison: in R22 may-minihttp beat hyper and axum but only matched Tokio-based actix-server and ntex-plt on plaintext, while in R23 it led hyper, axum, ntex-plt and xitca-web on plaintext, JSON and fortunes (derived from raw data).
status_note: Maintained (commits through 2026-08-03; latest crates.io releases may 0.3.51 on 2025-05-13 and may_minihttp 0.1.11 on 2024-09-22) and dual MIT/Apache-2.0 on crates.io; RustSec lists no advisory for may itself and old ones for its may_queue and generator dependencies are patched, but the documented TLS hazard (#6) and the open go! soundness issue (#109) make it better suited to controlled services than to general-purpose libraries.
